0.title: The Letter of Joy: Paul’s Letter to the Philippians
0.overview:
Philippians is the most personal and warmest of Paul’s letters — a love letter to the church that had been his closest partner in the gospel from the very beginning of the European mission. He wrote it from prison, most likely in Rome, facing the real possibility of execution. And yet the letter’s dominant note is joy. “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice” (4:4). The word “joy” or “rejoice” appears sixteen times in four chapters. This is not the forced cheerfulness of a man in denial; it is the deep, settled gladness of a man who has found that Christ is sufficient for every circumstance, including chains, including death.

Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia — the first European city Paul evangelized (Acts 16), where the gospel arrived through a riverside prayer meeting, a wealthy cloth merchant named Lydia, a slave girl freed from a spirit of divination, and a jailer shaken to conversion by an earthquake. The church that emerged from these unlikely beginnings remained Paul’s most generous supporter: “no church entered into partnership with me in giving and receiving except you only” (4:15). When Paul was imprisoned, they sent Epaphroditus with a gift — and now Paul sends this letter back with him, full of gratitude, theology, and pastoral instruction.

Where was Paul imprisoned when he wrote? Three places have been suggested. Some argue for Ephesus, because it was near enough to Philippi for the several journeys the letter implies; others for Caesarea, where Paul was held for two years (Acts 24:27). The more likely answer is Rome, around AD 60–62. Paul mentions the whole imperial guard (1:13) and those of Caesar’s household (4:22), and he faces a verdict that could end in death with no further appeal, which fits Rome, where he had already appealed to Caesar, better than either alternative.

The letter’s theological heart is the great Christ hymn of chapter 2 (vv. 6–11), which may be the earliest christological poem in the New Testament — pre-Pauline in origin, perhaps already sung in the churches before Paul wrote. It traces the arc of the Son of God from the heights of divine equality, through the descent of incarnation and the depths of a slave’s death on a cross, to the exaltation at which every knee bows and every tongue confesses. This is not merely doxology; it is the pattern of Christian existence. The community that sings this hymn is called to embody it: the same self-emptying, other-serving, glory-surrendering mind that was in Christ Jesus is to be in them.

The letter’s other great passage is the biographical testimony of chapter 3 (vv. 4–11), where Paul lists his impressive Jewish credentials — circumcised on the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, blameless under the law — and then counts them all as loss, as rubbish, as dung (skybala) compared to “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.” This is the gospel of grace arriving at personal address: not the abstract doctrine of justification but the lived reality of a man for whom Christ has become everything, and everything else has become nothing by comparison.

Philippians is the answer to the question: what does a life shaped by the gospel actually look like? It looks like partnership rather than rivalry, like humility rather than self-promotion, like contentment rather than anxiety, like pressing forward rather than dwelling on the past, like the peace of God that passes understanding rather than the turmoil of the person whose security rests on circumstances. It is the most beautiful portrait of mature Christian life in Paul’s letters — and it was painted by a man in chains, who could see the executioner’s sword, and who wrote: “to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”

1.title: To Live Is Christ: Partnership, Prison, and the Advance of the Gospel
1.overview:
Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, settled by retired soldiers, and the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16): a businesswoman named Lydia, a converted jailer, and a few others. About ten years later Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, to thank them for a gift and to steady them under opposition. It is the warmest of his letters, full of joy.

Chapter 1 thanks God for their partnership in the gospel and states a great certainty: God, who began a good work in them, will finish it. Paul prays that their love will grow in knowledge and discernment. Then he reports from his cell: his chains have advanced the gospel through the imperial guard, other believers have grown bolder, and even rivals who preach to spite him are preaching Christ, so he rejoices. Facing a possible death sentence, he writes, “to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain,” yet expects to stay for their sake. He ends by calling them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel, standing together, unafraid, knowing that suffering for Christ is itself a gift of grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul and Timothy greet the whole church at Philippi, including its overseers and deacons. Paul thanks God with joy every time he remembers them, because they have been his partners in the gospel from the first day, and he is sure that God, who began his work in them, will bring it to completion on the day of Christ. He carries them in his heart; they share in God’s grace with him in prison and in defending the gospel. His prayer is that their love will grow, guided by knowledge and discernment, so that they choose what matters most and are found pure and full of the fruit of righteousness on the last day, to God’s glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Finishes What He Starts

Philippians 1:6 is among the strongest statements of perseverance in the New Testament, and its whole force lies in the subject of the two verbs. God began the good work; God will complete it. The believer is the field, not the farmer. Reformed theology has always insisted that perseverance is not the Christian’s achievement but God’s gift — the same grace that opens a heart keeps it, and the same power that raised Christ is at work in everyone united to him.

This is not a doctrine that makes effort pointless; it is what makes effort reasonable. Paul will command the Philippians to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling, and in the same breath tell them that it is God who works in them both to will and to work (2:12–13). The two sentences are not in tension. A Christian labours precisely because the outcome is guaranteed by someone else, which is the only ground on which anyone has ever laboured with hope. Assurance rests not on the strength of our grip but on the certainty of his (John 10:28–29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Philippians had every reason for anxiety. Their apostle was in chains, their city was a Roman garrison town where the imperial cult was a civic expectation, opposition was real (v.28), and the congregation had a quarrel in it that Paul will have to name by the end of the letter (4:2). His answer is not to reassure them about their circumstances or to praise their track record, but to point them to the character of the God who started the work.

Now: The Christian who lies awake wondering whether his faith will last is asking a question about the wrong grip. If perseverance depends on the tenacity of the believer, the honest answer is bleak; every one of us has already discovered how quickly we let go. Verse 6 puts the question the other way round — will God let go? — and answers it with “I am sure of this.” And verse 9 supplies the prayer to pray for the people you love: not that their week would be easy, but that their love would grow eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Meaning first. Philippians is Paul’s most joyful letter, written from prison to the church he loved most. Its great theme is joy in Christ whatever the circumstances, and partnership in the gospel. Chapter 1 opens with warm thanksgiving for the Philippians’ partnership from the first day, confidence that God will finish the good work he began in them, and a prayer that their love will abound in knowledge and discernment (vv. 1–11). Then Paul explains his situation: his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel, spreading it through the imperial guard and emboldening other believers. Even those who preach out of rivalry are preaching Christ, so he rejoices (vv. 12–18). He faces possible death with calm: for to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. To depart and be with Christ would be far better, but remaining is better for them, and he expects to stay (vv. 19–26). Finally, he calls them to live as citizens worthy of the gospel, united, unafraid of opponents, knowing that God has granted them not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him (vv. 27–30).

Setting and background. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16:11–40). Founded by Philip II of Macedon and refounded as a colony for Roman army veterans after the battle of Philippi in 42 BC, it was proud of its Roman citizenship. The church began with Lydia, a slave girl set free from a spirit, and a jailer. Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62, though some suggest Ephesus or Caesarea. The Philippians had sent Epaphroditus with a gift (4:18).

Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus. Key words. “Servants” (douloi, slaves). No mention of apostleship, unlike most letters. No need to assert authority with this loving church.

To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi. Key words. “All” appears often in this letter (1:4, 7, 8, 25; 2:17), perhaps because there were tensions (4:2). Paul loves them all equally.

With the overseers and deacons. Key words. “Overseers” (episkopoi, from which bishop): elders who led and taught (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7). “Deacons” (diakonoi, servants): those who served practical needs (1 Timothy 3:8–13). Two offices in the local church, both plural.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. Paul’s standard greeting, from the Father and the Son together.

Where Christians differ: church government. Some churches have a bishop over many congregations, distinct from elders. Others have a single pastor with no elders. Verdict: In the New Testament, overseer and elder are the same office (Titus 1:5–7; Acts 20:17, 28), held by a plurality of qualified men in each church, with deacons serving alongside. The New Testament pattern is two offices, elders and deacons, with elders sharing leadership. Churches may organise their wider fellowship in various ways, but this local pattern is biblical.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church leaders are superior Christians. They are servants among servants.

In a sentence. From Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all God’s holy people in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for your church’s elders and deacons. Pray for them by name.
verseByVerse.note: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, the first church Paul founded in Europe. He wrote from prison, probably in Rome. “Overseers” (elders) and deacons were the two offices of leadership.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank my God in all my remembrance of you, always in every prayer of mine for you all making my prayer with joy, because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank my God in all my remembrance of you, always in every prayer of mine for you all making my prayer with joy, because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now.

I thank my God in all my remembrance of you. Key words. Every time Paul thinks of them, he thanks God. My God: personal.

Always in every prayer of mine for you all making my prayer with joy. Key words. Joy (chara) appears here for the first of sixteen times in the letter (with rejoice). Paul prays for them with joy, not burden.

Because of your partnership in the gospel. Key words. “Partnership” (koinōnia, fellowship, sharing, participation). The Philippians had supported Paul financially from the start (4:15–16), and shared in his work through prayer and sending workers. Gospel partnership is the heart of their relationship.

From the first day until now. Key words. From Lydia’s conversion (Acts 16:14–15) to the present gift. Ten years of faithful partnership.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only financial support counts as partnership. Prayer, encouragement and shared suffering are part of it too.

In a sentence. Paul thanks his God every time he remembers you. In all his prayers for all of you, he always prays with joy because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now.

For worship. Thank God for the gospel partners in your life: those who pray, give, and work with you for Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The Philippians had supported Paul financially from the start.

verseByVerse.quote: And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.

And I am sure of this. Key words. “Sure” (peithō, persuaded, confident). Paul’s confidence is not in them but in God.

That he who began a good work in you. Key words. God began it: salvation, their faith and their partnership. The good work is God’s saving work in them, from new birth onwards.

Will bring it to completion. Key words. “Bring to completion” (epiteleō, finish, perfect). God finishes what he starts.

At the day of Jesus Christ. Key words. Christ’s return, when the work will be complete: glorification.

Where Christians differ: the perseverance of the saints. Some teach that believers can fall away and be finally lost. Verdict: Paul is confident that God will complete the work he began. Salvation rests on God’s faithfulness, not our grip. True believers may stumble badly, but God will keep them to the end (John 6:39; 10:28–29; Romans 8:30). This is the perseverance of the saints, better called the preservation of the saints by God (Westminster 17.1–2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are passive. God works in us as we work out our salvation (2:12–13).

In a sentence. And Paul is confident of this: he who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. When you feel you are failing as a Christian, remember: God started the work, and he will finish it.

verseByVerse.quote: It is right for me to feel this way about you all, because I hold you in my heart, for you are all partakers with me of grace, both in my imprisonment and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel. For God is my witness, how I yearn for you all with the affection of Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is right for me to feel this way about you all, because I hold you in my heart, for you are all partakers with me of grace, both in my imprisonment and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel. For God is my witness, how I yearn for you all with the affection of Christ Jesus.

It is right for me to feel this way about you all. Key words. Paul’s confidence and love are justified.

Because I hold you in my heart. Key words. They are deeply loved. Some take it as: because you hold me in your heart.

For you are all partakers with me of grace. Key words. “Partakers” (synkoinōnoi, fellow sharers). They share in God’s grace with Paul.

Both in my imprisonment and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel. Key words. They supported him in prison and stood with him in defending the gospel. “Defense” (apologia) and “confirmation” (bebaiōsis): legal terms. Paul may have been preparing his defence before Caesar.

For God is my witness, how I yearn for you all with the affection of Christ Jesus. Key words. “Yearn” (epipotheō, long for). “Affection” (splanchna, inner feelings, heart). Paul loves them with Christ’s own love, flowing through him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s love was mere emotion. It was Christ’s love, shown in action.

In a sentence. It is right for Paul to feel this way about all of you, since he has you in his heart, and, whether he is in chains or defending and confirming the gospel, all of you share in God’s grace with him. God can testify how he longs for all of you with the affection of Christ Jesus.

For worship. Ask Christ to fill you with his affection for the believers in your church.

verseByVerse.quote: And it is my prayer that your love may abound more and more, with knowledge and all discernment, so that you may approve what is excellent, and so be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it is my prayer that your love may abound more and more, with knowledge and all discernment, so that you may approve what is excellent, and so be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

And it is my prayer that your love may abound more and more. Key words. Their love is already strong; Paul prays for more. Love can always grow.

With knowledge and all discernment. Key words. Love must be informed. “Knowledge” (epignōsis, full knowledge, especially of God). “Discernment” (aisthēsis, moral perception, sensitivity). Love without knowledge can be sentimental or misguided.

So that you may approve what is excellent. Key words. “Approve” (dokimazō, test and approve). “What is excellent” (ta diapheronta, the things that differ, the things that matter). Not just good versus bad, but good versus best.

And so be pure and blameless for the day of Christ. Key words. “Pure” (eilikrinēs, sincere, tested by sunlight). “Blameless” (aproskopos, not causing others to stumble).

Filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ. Key words. Righteous living, which comes from Christ, not from our own effort (Galatians 5:22; John 15:5).

To the glory and praise of God. Key words. The goal of all growth.

What it does not mean. It does not mean knowledge replaces love. It means knowledge guides love.

In a sentence. And this is Paul’s prayer: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight, so that you may be able to discern what is best and may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

On a Tuesday. Pray this prayer for someone you love today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Chains, the Rivals, and the Choice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reports that his imprisonment has helped the gospel rather than hindered it. The imperial guard knows why he is in chains, and other believers have grown bolder. Some preach Christ out of rivalry, hoping to hurt him; others out of love. He rejoices either way, because Christ is being proclaimed. He expects, through their prayers and the Spirit’s help, that all this will turn out for his good, and his one hope is that Christ will be honoured in his body whether he lives or dies. Living means Christ; dying would be gain. Torn between departing to be with Christ and staying for their sake, he is convinced he will remain, for their progress and joy in the faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence: The Chains Were Not a Setback

What Paul reports here is Romans 8:28 in biographical form. God’s providence is not merely reactive — not the salvaging of a situation that got away from him — but his active government of all things, including hostile human choices, toward his own redemptive ends. The Roman legal machinery believed it had detained Paul. Paul knew he had been stationed (v.16, keimai). Same cell, two accounts of the world.

The same doctrine governs his response to the rival preachers, and its limits need stating precisely. Paul is not indifferent to motive — he names theirs as envy and selfish ambition, and forbids that spirit in the Philippian church in the next chapter (2:3). Nor is he indifferent to content; the man who wrote Galatians 1:8 would anathematise a preacher of another gospel. His point is narrower and sturdier: where the message is true, its power lies in the message and not in the messenger, and God is not so fastidious as to let a soul perish rather than use a flawed instrument.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul writes as a prisoner whose usefulness looked finished, to a church that was funding a mission which appeared to have stalled. He gives them no general assurance that things work out. He gives them a report: here is what God has in fact done with the wreckage — a guard evangelised, a church emboldened, and a gospel travelling on roads nobody had planned.

Now: Two applications, and they pull in different directions. For the believer whose life has been derailed — the illness that ended the work, the split that closed the ministry — verse 12 is not a demand to feel that the loss was a gain. And for the believer who is afraid to die, verses 21–23 offer not a stoic’s courage but an accountant’s logic: whether death is gain depends entirely on what you have made your life. Fill in Paul’s blank — for to me to live is — and the word that arrives unbidden will tell you what you have built on.

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel, so that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard and to all the rest that my imprisonment is for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel, so that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard and to all the rest that my imprisonment is for Christ.

I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me. Key words. His arrest and imprisonment.

Has really served to advance the gospel. Key words. “Advance” (prokopē, progress, a word used of pioneers cutting a way through forest). What looked like defeat became progress.

So that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard. Key words. The ESV notes that “imperial guard” is literally the whole praetorium: the elite Praetorian Guard in Rome, or the governor’s headquarters elsewhere. Paul was chained to a different soldier each shift. Each one heard the gospel.

And to all the rest that my imprisonment is for Christ. Key words. Everyone knows he is not a criminal but a prisoner for Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering is good in itself. It means God uses it to advance his purposes.

In a sentence. Now Paul wants you to know, brothers and sisters, that what has happened to him has actually served to advance the gospel. As a result, it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that he is in chains for Christ.

For worship. Ask God to use your difficult circumstances to advance the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “imperial guard” is literally “the whole praetorium” — the Roman soldiers guarding him, or the governor’s headquarters.

verseByVerse.quote: And most of the brothers, having become confident in the Lord by my imprisonment, are much more bold to speak the word without fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And most of the brothers, having become confident in the Lord by my imprisonment, are much more bold to speak the word without fear.

And most of the brothers, having become confident in the Lord by my imprisonment. Key words. Seeing Paul’s faithfulness in chains gave others courage.

Are much more bold to speak the word without fear. Key words. “Without fear” (aphobōs). Paul’s suffering emboldened the church. Courage is contagious.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fear disappeared entirely. It means faith overcame it.

In a sentence. And because of Paul’s chains, most of the brothers and sisters have become confident in the Lord and dare all the more to proclaim the gospel without fear.

On a Tuesday. Your faithfulness in hard times may give others courage. Be brave for their sake.

verseByVerse.quote: Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will. The latter do it out of love, knowing that I am put here for the defense of the gospel. The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me in my imprisonment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will. The latter do it out of love, knowing that I am put here for the defense of the gospel. The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me in my imprisonment.

Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry. Key words. Some preachers in Rome were jealous of Paul and saw his imprisonment as their chance to gain influence.

But others from good will. Key words. Others preached with love.

The latter do it out of love, knowing that I am put here for the defense of the gospel. Key words. They understood Paul’s imprisonment as God’s appointment.

The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely. Key words. “Selfish ambition” (eritheia, party spirit, self-promotion). Their motives were wrong, but their message was right. Unlike the Galatian false teachers, they preached the true Christ.

But thinking to afflict me in my imprisonment. Key words. They hoped to make Paul jealous or to increase his troubles.

What it does not mean. It does not mean motives do not matter. God judges motives (1 Corinthians 4:5). It means the true gospel can be preached even by flawed people.

In a sentence. It is true that some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill. The latter do so out of love, knowing that Paul is put here for the defence of the gospel. The former preach Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely, supposing that they can stir up trouble for him while he is in chains.

For worship. Examine your motives in serving Christ. Ask God to purify them.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice,
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice,

What then? Key words. So what?

Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed. Key words. “Pretense” (prophasis, pretext, false motive). The message is true, even if the motive is not.

And in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will rejoice. Key words. Paul does not care about his own reputation, only that Christ is preached. A remarkable freedom from self.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul accepted false gospels. He condemns them fiercely (Galatians 1:8). Here the content is true; only the motives are wrong.

In a sentence. But what does it matter? The important thing is that in every way, whether from false motives or true, Christ is preached. And because of this Paul rejoices. Yes, and he will continue to rejoice,

On a Tuesday. When others get credit for gospel work, rejoice that Christ is preached. Let go of your own reputation.

verseByVerse.quote: for I know that through your prayers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ this will turn out for my deliverance,
verseByVerse.commentary:
for I know that through your prayers and the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ this will turn out for my deliverance,

For I know that through your prayers. Key words. The Philippians’ prayers are part of God’s means.

And the help of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. Key words. “Help” (epichorēgia, supply, provision). The Spirit supplies what Paul needs. The Spirit of Jesus Christ: the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:9).

This will turn out for my deliverance. Key words. Echoes Job 13:16 in the Greek translation. “Deliverance” (sōtēria, salvation). Either release from prison, or final salvation and vindication, whatever happens. Verse 20 suggests the latter: whether he lives or dies, he will be vindicated.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was sure he would be released. He was sure God would bring good out of it.

In a sentence. for he knows that through your prayers and God’s provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ what has happened to him will turn out for his deliverance.

For worship. Pray for believers in prison for their faith. Your prayers matter.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be at all ashamed, but that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
as it is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be at all ashamed, but that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

As it is my eager expectation and hope. Key words. “Eager expectation” (apokaradokia, watching with outstretched neck, as in Romans 8:19).

That I will not be at all ashamed. Key words. Not disgraced by failing Christ at his trial.

But that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body. Key words. “Honoured” (megalynō, magnified, made great). Like a magnifying glass making Christ look great.

Whether by life or by death. Key words. If released, he will serve Christ; if executed, he will die well for Christ. Either way, Christ is magnified.

For to me to live is Christ. Key words. Life means Christ: knowing him, serving him, loving him. Christ is the content, purpose and goal of his life.

And to die is gain. Key words. Death means more of Christ: being with him (v. 23). For the one who lives for Christ, death is not loss but gain.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wished to die or despised this life. He saw both as good, because Christ is in both.

In a sentence. Paul eagerly expects and hopes that he will in no way be ashamed, but will have sufficient courage so that now as always Christ will be exalted in his body, whether by life or by death. For to him, to live is Christ and to die is gain.

For worship. Fill in the blank honestly: for me to live is ____. Ask God to make the answer Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account.

If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me. Key words. Living means more gospel fruit.

Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. Key words. Paul does not mean he controls his fate. He means he cannot say which he prefers.

I am hard pressed between the two. Key words. “Hard pressed” (synechō, squeezed, pulled both ways).

My desire is to depart and be with Christ. Key words. “Depart” (analyō, untie, unloose, as a ship leaving harbour or soldiers striking camp). Death is departure to be with Christ, immediately.

For that is far better. Key words. Literally, much more better. Being with Christ beats everything this life offers.

But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account. Key words. Love for others keeps Paul willing to stay.

Where Christians differ: the intermediate state. Some say the dead sleep unconsciously until the resurrection. Verdict: Paul says to depart is to be with Christ, and that is far better. That would not be far better if it were unconscious sleep. Believers who die go immediately into Christ’s conscious presence, where they await the resurrection of the body (2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43; Westminster 32.1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean suicide is acceptable. Paul leaves the timing to God.

In a sentence. If he is to go on living in the body, this will mean fruitful labour for him. Yet what shall he choose? He does not know! He is torn between the two: he desires to depart and be with Christ, which is better by far; but it is more necessary for you that he remain in the body.

On a Tuesday. If being with Christ is far better, you need not fear death. And while you live, labour fruitfully for others.

verseByVerse.quote: Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith, so that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith, so that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again.

Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all. Key words. Paul expects to be released. He probably was, and travelled again before a second imprisonment and death (1 Timothy 1:3; Titus 1:5; 2 Timothy 4:6).

For your progress and joy in the faith. Key words. “Progress” (prokopē, the same word as v. 12). His goal: their growth and joy.

So that in me you may have ample cause to glory in Christ Jesus, because of my coming to you again. Key words. His return would give them reason to rejoice, in Christ, not in Paul.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul had a guarantee from God. He had a strong conviction.

In a sentence. Convinced of this, he knows that he will remain, and he will continue with all of you for your progress and joy in the faith, so that through his being with you again your boasting in Christ Jesus will abound on account of him.

For worship. Thank God for those whose lives help your progress and joy in the faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul calls them to live as citizens whose conduct matches the gospel, standing together in one spirit and contending side by side for the faith, unafraid of their opponents. Their courage will be a sign of the opponents’ ruin and of their own salvation from God. Suffering for Christ, like believing in him, is something God has graciously given them, and they are now in the same struggle they once saw Paul endure.
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as a Grace-Gift

That suffering for Christ is granted — echaristhe, from charis, grace — is one of the most counter-intuitive claims in the New Testament. Not that God permits it, or merely redeems it after the fact, but that he bestows it, as he bestows faith, on those who belong to his Son. The apostles understood this when they left the Sanhedrin rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name (Acts 5:41).

Reformed theology has never treated suffering for the gospel as an aberration in the Christian life but as a feature of it in this present age: through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom (Acts 14:22). Union with a crucified and risen Lord means fellowship in both his death and his resurrection (3:10); the one cannot be taken and the other refused. A gospel that promises exemption from all hardship has misread the gift it is offering.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philippi was a garrison colony where loyalty to the emperor was ordinary civic decency, and confessing another Lord was a visible social defection. The opposition these believers faced was not random hostility; it was the predictable friction of two citizenships in one city. Paul answers it by telling them which capital they actually belong to — a point he will make explicit at 3:20.

Now: Verse 28 forbids the bolt, not the fear; a believer who is frightened and stays put has obeyed it. And it is composure under opposition for the gospel, not opposition as such, that counts as evidence — and even that is credited to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel,

Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ. Key words. The word for “manner of life” (politeuomai) means living as a citizen: fitting for a Roman colony proud of its citizenship. Believers are citizens of heaven (3:20); live as worthy citizens.

So that whether I come and see you or am absent. Key words. Whatever happens to Paul.

I may hear of you that you are standing firm in one spirit. Key words. “Standing firm” (stēkō), like soldiers holding their ground.

With one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel. Key words. “Striving side by side” (synathleō, contending together, as athletes on one team). United in the fight for the gospel. The faith of the gospel: the truth of the gospel believed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean uniformity of personality. It means unity of purpose.

In a sentence. Whatever happens, conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ. Then, whether Paul comes and sees you or only hears about you in his absence, he will know that you stand firm in the one Spirit, striving together as one for the faith of the gospel

On a Tuesday. You are a citizen of heaven. Live today in a way that fits your citizenship.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “manner of life” means living as a citizen — fitting for a Roman colony proud of its status.

verseByVerse.quote: and not frightened in anything by your opponents. This is a clear sign to them of their destruction, but of your salvation, and that from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and not frightened in anything by your opponents. This is a clear sign to them of their destruction, but of your salvation, and that from God.

And not frightened in anything by your opponents. Key words. “Frightened” (ptyrō, startled, as a horse shies). The Philippians faced opposition, perhaps from pagans and the Roman authorities.

This is a clear sign to them of their destruction. Key words. The believers’ fearless courage is a sign to opponents that they are fighting a losing battle against God.

But of your salvation, and that from God. Key words. And it is a sign to believers that they are truly saved. Courage under persecution is evidence of God’s work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never feel fear. It means faith overcomes it.

In a sentence. without being frightened in any way by those who oppose you. This is a sign to them that they will be destroyed, but that you will be saved, and that by God.

For worship. Ask God for courage in the face of opposition. Your calm faith is a testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: For it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake, engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had and now hear that I still have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it has been granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake, engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had and now hear that I still have.

For it has been granted to you. Key words. “Granted” (charizomai, given as a gift of grace). Two gifts follow.

That for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him. Key words. Faith is a gift of God’s grace (Ephesians 2:8; Acts 13:48).

But also suffer for his sake. Key words. Suffering for Christ is also a gift: a privilege of sharing his sufferings (Acts 5:41; 1 Peter 4:13).

Engaged in the same conflict that you saw I had and now hear that I still have. Key words. Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed at Philippi (Acts 16:19–24). The Philippians saw it. Now they share the same struggle.

Where Christians differ: is faith a gift? Some say faith is our own contribution, the one thing we bring to God. Verdict: Paul says believing in Christ was granted, given by grace. Faith is our act, but it is God’s gift, produced by the Spirit in regeneration (Ephesians 2:8–9; John 6:44, 65). So even faith gives no ground for boasting. This is effectual calling: God gives the faith he requires (Westminster 14.1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God forces people to believe. He changes the heart so that they gladly believe.

In a sentence. For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him, since you are going through the same struggle you saw Paul had, and now hear that he still has.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the gift of faith. And if you suffer for Christ, see it as a privilege, not a punishment.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Silas had been beaten and jailed at Philippi.

2.title: The Mind of Christ: Humility, the Incarnation, and the Cross
2.overview:
Chapter 1 ended with a church under pressure from outside. Chapter 2 turns to the pressure inside: rivalry, conceit and grumbling, the kind of thing that later surfaces in two named women who cannot agree (4:2). Paul’s answer is not a management technique but a person. He sets before them the mind of Christ, in what may be the most important paragraph on the incarnation in the Bible (2:6–11): the one who was in the form of God did not use his equality with God for his own advantage, but emptied himself by taking the form of a slave, obeyed to the point of a slave’s death on a cross, and was therefore exalted by God to the name above every name, so that every knee will bow to him as the Lord of Isaiah 45.

Then come the consequences. Work out your salvation, because God is working in you. Stop grumbling, as Israel grumbled in the wilderness, and shine like stars in a twisted generation. Paul himself may be poured out as a drink offering, and is glad. The chapter closes with two portraits of the same mind in ordinary men: Timothy, who genuinely cares for others when everyone else looks after themselves, and Epaphroditus, the church’s courier, who nearly died bringing their gift and was more upset that they had heard he was ill than that he was.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Appealing to all they have received in Christ, Paul asks them to complete his joy by being united in love and purpose, acting not from rivalry or vanity but humbly putting others first and caring for their interests. The attitude he wants is the one that belongs to them in Christ, and he describes it in a great passage about Christ himself. Though truly God, Christ did not use his equality with God for his own advantage. He emptied himself by taking the nature of a slave and becoming human, and then humbled himself further, obeying all the way to death on a cross. So God has raised him to the highest place and given him the supreme name, so that all creation will bow to him and confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the Father’s glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Kenosis: What the Son Laid Aside, and What He Did Not

Verse 7 is the classic text for the incarnation, and its most important feature is grammatical: “he emptied himself” has no object. Paul does not say what the Son emptied himself of. He explains the emptying by what follows — “by taking the form of a servant.” The kenosis is therefore not subtraction but addition. He did not become less than God; he took to himself what he had never possessed, a full human nature.

What was laid aside was the independent exercise of divine prerogatives — the free use of what remained fully his. The glory was veiled rather than surrendered, and broke out once on the mountain to prove it had been there all along (Mark 9:2–3). This is Chalcedonian orthodoxy, which the Reformed tradition has always confessed: two natures in one person, without confusion and without division. He was not less than God in the manger, and not less than man on the cross.

Verses 10–11 raise a second question that must be answered honestly. Every knee bowing does not mean everyone is saved; the same letter speaks of opponents whose end is destruction (1:28; 3:19). Isaiah 45 itself distinguishes those who come gladly from those who come to him ashamed. Universal acknowledgement is certain; universal salvation is not taught here. The question the passage puts to the reader is not whether he will bow, but when — and in which posture.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philippi had a status problem. Two women in the congregation could not agree (4:2), and the vocabulary Paul reaches for — eritheia, selfish ambition, the same word he used of the rival preachers in 1:17 — suggests the quarrel was less about doctrine than about position. Into that he drops the deepest thing he knows: the one with the highest claim in the universe declined to press it.

Now: The useful question in verse 6 is not “do I have a right here?” In most church conflicts you probably do. It is what you intend to do with the right you have. And verse 3 asks for a decision rather than a feeling: to count others more significant is a verb of judgement, a reckoning, not an emotion you must manufacture. Think of the person you find hardest in your congregation. Humility is not pretending you find them easy; it is deciding, before the next conversation, that what they need from it matters more than what you want from it.

verseByVerse.quote: So if there is any encouragement in Christ, any comfort from love, any participation in the Spirit, any affection and sympathy, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So if there is any encouragement in Christ, any comfort from love, any participation in the Spirit, any affection and sympathy, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind.

Meaning first. Philippians 2 contains one of the greatest passages in the Bible about Christ, and Paul uses it for an intensely practical purpose: unity and humility in the church. First, he appeals to them to be of one mind, doing nothing out of selfish ambition, but in humility counting others more significant (vv. 1–4). Then he gives the supreme example: Christ Jesus, who was in the form of God, did not cling to his equality with God, but emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, became man, and humbled himself to death on a cross. Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (vv. 5–11). Next, Paul calls them to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, because God is at work in them; to do everything without grumbling, shining like stars in a twisted world (vv. 12–18). Finally, he commends two men who embody Christ’s mind: Timothy, who genuinely cares for them, and Epaphroditus, who nearly died serving Christ (vv. 19–30).

So if there is any encouragement in Christ. Key words. Four “if” clauses, each meaning “since”: since there is. Encouragement (paraklēsis) in Christ: the strengthening that comes from union with him.

Any comfort from love. Key words. “Comfort” (paramythion, consolation, soothing). The comfort of Christ’s love.

Any participation in the Spirit. Key words. “Participation” (koinōnia, fellowship). Shared life in the one Spirit.

Any affection and sympathy. Key words. “Affection” (splanchna, tender feelings) and “sympathy” (oiktirmoi, compassion).

Complete my joy by being of the same mind. Key words. Paul’s joy will be full when they are united. “Same mind” (to auto phronēte, think the same thing). The word phroneō, thinking, mindset, is a key word in Philippians (ten times).

Having the same love, being in full accord and of one mind. Key words. “Full accord” (sympsychos, one-souled). Unity of heart and purpose. There were tensions in the church (4:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean agreeing on every opinion. It means one shared mindset: the mind of Christ (v. 5).

In a sentence. Therefore if you have any encouragement from being united with Christ, if any comfort from his love, if any common sharing in the Spirit, if any tenderness and compassion, then make Paul’s joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being one in spirit and of one mind.

On a Tuesday. Is there a broken relationship in your church? Work for unity, for Christ’s sake.

verseByVerse.quote: Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.

Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit. Key words. “Selfish ambition” (eritheia, party spirit, self-promotion, as in 1:17). “Conceit” (kenodoxia, empty glory, vainglory). The two great enemies of unity.

But in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Key words. “Humility” (tapeinophrosynē, lowly-mindedness). In Greek culture, humility was a slave’s trait, not a virtue. Christ made it a virtue. “Count” (hēgeomai, consider, regard). Deliberately treat others as more important. Not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less.

Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others. Key words. “Look” (skopeō, watch, aim at). Not ignore your own needs, but give attention to others’.

What it does not mean. It does not mean false modesty or denying your gifts. It means putting others first.

In a sentence. Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves, not looking to your own interests but each of you to the interests of the others.

For worship. Ask God to give you a humble heart that seeks others’ good.

verseByVerse.quote: Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus,

Have this mind among yourselves. Key words. “Mind” (phroneō, attitude, way of thinking). Think this way, together, as a community.

Which is yours in Christ Jesus. Key words. Either: which was in Christ Jesus (the example to copy), or: which is yours because you are in Christ Jesus (the new identity to live out). Both are true. The mind of Christ is our model and our possession.

The Christ hymn. Verses 6–11 may be an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung in worship before Paul wrote, or composed by Paul. It has a poetic structure: Christ’s descent (vv. 6–8) and his exaltation (vv. 9–11). It is among the earliest and highest statements of Christ’s deity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can copy Christ’s atoning work. We copy his attitude.

In a sentence. In your relationships with one another, have the same mindset as Christ Jesus:

On a Tuesday. In every decision today, ask: what would the humble mind of Christ do?
verseByVerse.note: Verses 6–11 may be an early Christian hymn.

verseByVerse.quote: who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped,
verseByVerse.commentary:
who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped,

Who, though he was in the form of God. Key words. “Was” (hyparchōn, existing, being): his continual state before the incarnation. “Form” (morphē): not just appearance, but the outward expression of what one truly is. Christ possessed the nature of God, with all its glory. He was, and is, God.

Did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped. Key words. “Equality with God” (isa theō): he was equal with God. “A thing to be grasped” (harpagmos, something to seize, or to hold on to and exploit). He did not regard his equality with God as something to cling to for his own advantage. Unlike Adam, who grasped at being like God (Genesis 3:5), Christ, who was God, did not grasp.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ was not equal with God and tried to become so. He was equal, and did not use it for himself.

In a sentence. Who, being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage;

For worship. Worship Jesus as God, equal with the Father, who chose not to cling to his rights for your sake.

verseByVerse.quote: but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men.

But emptied himself. Key words. “Emptied” (kenoō, made himself nothing, poured out). From which kenosis. What did he empty himself of? Paul explains: by taking the form of a servant. He emptied himself not by subtracting his deity but by adding humanity, and by setting aside the privileges and glory he had a right to.

By taking the form of a servant. Key words. The same word “form” (morphē) as verse 6. He truly became a servant (doulos, slave), as truly as he was God. The highest became the lowest.

Being born in the likeness of men. Key words. “Likeness” (homoiōma). He became truly human, like us in every way except sin (Hebrews 2:17; 4:15).

Where Christians differ: what did Christ empty himself of? Kenotic theories teach that the Son gave up some divine attributes, such as omniscience or omnipotence, when he became man. Verdict: The Son did not cease to be God or lose any divine attribute; God cannot stop being God. He emptied himself by taking human nature and the role of a servant, veiling his glory and not using his divine rights for his own benefit. He remained fully God while becoming fully man, two natures in one person, without confusion or change (Chalcedonian Definition; Westminster 8.2). During his earthly life, he chose to depend on the Spirit and the Father.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ was only part God or only part man. He is fully both.

In a sentence. rather, he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness.

For worship. Marvel at the humility of God the Son becoming a servant. Bow before him.

parallels.desc: he poured out his soul to death

verseByVerse.quote: And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.

And being found in human form. Key words. “Form” here is schēma, outward appearance. He looked like any other man.

He humbled himself. Key words. “Humbled” (tapeinoō, made himself low). A second step down. Becoming man was humbling; he went lower still.

By becoming obedient to the point of death. Key words. He obeyed the Father perfectly, all the way, even to death (Hebrews 5:8; John 10:18). His obedience is our righteousness (Romans 5:19).

Even death on a cross. Key words. Crucifixion was the most shameful form of Roman execution, reserved for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals. Roman citizens, like many in Philippi, could not be crucified. Cicero said the very word cross should be far from a Roman’s thoughts. And it meant God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23). The lowest point in the universe.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the cross was only an example of humility. It was the atoning sacrifice for sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). But it is also the supreme example.

In a sentence. And being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross!

For worship. Look at the cross and see how low Christ went for you. Thank him.
verseByVerse.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful form of Roman execution.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

Therefore God has highly exalted him. Key words. “Highly exalted” (hyperypsoō, super-exalted). Because of his humility, God raised him to the highest place: resurrection, ascension, enthronement at God’s right hand (Acts 2:33; Ephesians 1:20–21).

And bestowed on him the name that is above every name. Key words. The name: Lord (kyrios), the Greek translation of God’s own name, Yahweh. The name above every name.

So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth. Key words. The words echo a passage where the LORD says every knee will bow to him alone (Isaiah 45:23). Paul applies it to Jesus. In heaven: angels. On earth: humans. Under the earth: the dead, and perhaps demons. All creation.

And every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Key words. The earliest Christian creed: Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3).

To the glory of God the Father. Key words. Honouring the Son glorifies the Father (John 5:23).

Where Christians differ: will everyone be saved? Some read this as meaning every person will eventually confess Christ willingly and be saved. Verdict: Every knee will bow and every tongue confess, but not all willingly or savingly. Some will confess in joyful worship; others will be compelled to acknowledge his lordship at the judgement (Romans 14:10–11; Revelation 20:11–15). Isaiah 45:24 adds that his enemies will come to him and be ashamed. This is the universal acknowledgement of Christ’s lordship, not universal salvation. Hell is real and eternal (Matthew 25:46).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus became God at his exaltation. He was always in the form of God (v. 6). He was exalted as the God-man, the Mediator.

In a sentence. Therefore God exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue acknowledge that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

On a Tuesday. Bow your knee to Jesus today, willingly and joyfully. One day everyone will.
verseByVerse.note: The words echo a passage where the LORD says every knee will bow to him alone; Paul applies them to Jesus.

parallels.desc: to me every knee shall bow

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — Working Out What God Works In
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges them, now that he is absent, to keep working out their salvation with reverent seriousness, because God himself is at work in them, giving both the desire and the power to do his will. They are to stop grumbling and arguing, so that, like stars in a dark sky, they shine with blameless lives in a twisted world as they hold on to the message of life. Then Paul will know on the last day that his work among them was not wasted. Even if his life is poured out like a drink offering on their faith, he is glad, and they should share his gladness.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sovereignty and Responsibility in Sanctification

Verses 12–13 are the New Testament’s most exact statement of how holiness actually works, and the decisive word is the little conjunction between them. Paul does not write “work out your salvation, but remember God is working too,” as though effort and grace divided the task between them. He writes work, for God is at work. Divine agency is the ground of human effort, not its rival. The two do not compete for the same square inch; they rise and fall together.

And the working-in reaches further than the ability to obey: God works “both to will and to work.” He is beneath the desire itself. A Christian who finds in himself a genuine wish to please God is looking at evidence of grace, not of good character. This is why “fear and trembling” is the fitting posture — not the dread that God might drop him, which 1:6 has already excluded, but the seriousness of a man who has realised whose workshop he is standing in. Note also that every pronoun here is plural: Paul is telling a congregation with a quarrel in it to work this out together.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Philippians had a good record of obedience, but it had been built with an apostle available. Paul’s concern is what happens now that he is in chains and may never return — and the first sin he names is the wilderness sin of murmuring.

Now: Grumbling is the respectable Christian’s sin, and almost no one repents of it. Verse 13 is the word for the believer who feels the gap between who he is and who he longs to be: the longing itself is God’s doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, so now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.

Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed. Key words. Therefore: in the light of Christ’s example. They have been obedient.

So now, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence. Key words. Their obedience is not to Paul but to God.

Work out your own salvation. Key words. “Work out” (katergazomai, carry through to completion). Not work for salvation, but work it out: live out what God has worked in. In context, includes working out their life together as a community, in unity.

With fear and trembling. Key words. Reverent awe before God, and humble dependence (1 Corinthians 2:3; Ephesians 6:5). Not terror, but seriousness.

For it is God who works in you. Key words. The reason we can work: God is working. “Works” (energeō, energises, is at work).

Both to will and to work for his good pleasure. Key words. God gives both the desire and the ability. He works in our will and in our action. All for his good pleasure.

Where Christians differ: God’s work and ours. Some say sanctification is all God’s work and we are passive; others that it is all our effort. Verdict: Both are fully true. God works in us; therefore we work out. Our working does not compete with his; it is the result of his. This is not cooperation as equal partners, but our real activity flowing from his prior and deeper work (Westminster 16.3). We pray as if everything depends on God, and work because God is working.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on our effort. It is God’s work from start to finish. But it is lived out through our effort.

In a sentence. Therefore, dear friends, as you have always obeyed, not only in Paul’s presence but now much more in his absence, continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you to will and to act in order to fulfil his good purpose.

On a Tuesday. Work hard at obedience today, knowing that God is working in you. Every good desire and action is his gift.

verseByVerse.quote: Do all things without grumbling or disputing,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do all things without grumbling or disputing,

Do all things without grumbling. Key words. “Grumbling” (gongysmos, murmuring, muttering complaint). Like Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8; Numbers 14:27; 1 Corinthians 10:10). Grumbling against God, leaders or one another.

Or disputing. Key words. “Disputing” (dialogismos, arguing, questioning). Quarrelsome arguments that divide.

What it does not mean. It does not mean never expressing concerns or lament. It means rejecting a complaining spirit.

In a sentence. Do everything without grumbling or arguing,

For worship. Replace one complaint today with thanksgiving.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labor in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast to the word of life, so that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labor in vain.

That you may be blameless and innocent. Key words. “Blameless” (amemptos): no just cause for blame. “Innocent” (akeraios, unmixed, pure).

Children of God without blemish. Key words. “Without blemish” (amōmos), the word for unblemished sacrifices.

In the midst of a crooked and twisted generation. Key words. From Deuteronomy 32:5, where Israel was the crooked generation. Now it describes the unbelieving world. Believers live in the middle of it, not withdrawn from it.

Among whom you shine as lights in the world. Key words. “Lights” (phōstēres, stars, luminaries, as in Genesis 1:14). Echoes Daniel 12:3: the wise will shine like the stars. Believers shine against the darkness (Matthew 5:14–16).

Holding fast to the word of life. Key words. Or: holding out the word of life. Both: hold it firmly, and offer it to others. The gospel gives life.

So that in the day of Christ I may be proud that I did not run in vain or labor in vain. Key words. Their faithfulness will prove Paul’s work was not wasted.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians are sinless. It means their lives should be visibly different.

In a sentence. so that you may become blameless and pure, children of God without fault in a warped and crooked generation. Then you will shine among them like stars in the sky as you hold firmly to the word of life. And then Paul will be able to boast on the day of Christ that he did not run or labour in vain.

On a Tuesday. Shine today in your workplace, home or neighbourhood. Hold out the word of life.

parallels.desc: those who are wise shall shine

verseByVerse.quote: Even if I am to be poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrificial offering of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all. Likewise you also should be glad and rejoice with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even if I am to be poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrificial offering of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with you all. Likewise you also should be glad and rejoice with me.

Even if I am to be poured out as a drink offering. Key words. A drink offering was wine poured out with a sacrifice, completing it (Numbers 28:7). Paul pictures his possible death as his life poured out (2 Timothy 4:6).

Upon the sacrificial offering of your faith. Key words. Their faith and service are the main sacrifice offered to God (Romans 12:1). Paul’s death would be the small addition poured over it.

I am glad and rejoice with you all. Key words. Even facing death, he rejoices.

Likewise you also should be glad and rejoice with me. Key words. They should not grieve but rejoice with him. Joy is the keynote of the letter.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s death atones for anything. It is an offering of thanks, not of atonement.

In a sentence. But even if Paul is being poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service coming from your faith, he is glad and rejoices with all of you. So you too should be glad and rejoice with him.

For worship. Offer your life to God as a sacrifice of thanks. Rejoice in it.
verseByVerse.note: A drink offering was wine poured out with a sacrifice, completing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–30 — Two Men Who Show You the Mind of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul hopes to send Timothy soon to bring back news of them. No one else shares his concern for them so genuinely; others are taken up with their own affairs, but Timothy has proved himself, serving with Paul in the gospel like a son with his father. Paul himself hopes to come later. Meanwhile he is sending back Epaphroditus, the man they sent to look after him, who fell ill and nearly died, but whom God spared, sparing Paul grief upon grief. Epaphroditus is homesick and upset that they heard he was ill, so Paul sends him gladly and asks them to welcome and honour him, because he risked his life for Christ’s work to do for Paul what they could not.
verseByVerse.theology:
Virtue Has to Be Seen in a Face

Reformed ethics has never treated Christian character as an abstraction. It is a way of living that exists only in particular people, and Paul’s method here follows his Lord’s: after the doctrine, a person. Timothy embodies 2:4 — looking to the interests of others — and Epaphroditus embodies 2:7–8, pouring himself out to the point of nearly dying. Neither is presented as an exceptional case. They are what the gospel ordinarily produces in people it has actually got hold of.

Two pastoral truths sit inside this section and should not be missed. First, Paul could not heal Epaphroditus. The apostle through whom God worked extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12) here watched a friend nearly die and credited the recovery to mercy alone. Healing is a gift God gives as he chooses, never a technique the church operates. Second, Paul admits to sorrow, and to sorrow that could have been piled upon sorrow. The man who wrote “rejoice always” was carrying grief while he wrote it. Joy in this letter runs underneath sadness; it does not replace it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Epaphroditus had been sent from Philippi to stay and serve, and was returning early, ill and with the job unfinished. Every congregation contains people ready to draw conclusions about that. Paul heads them off before the man reaches the gate — he is not coming back a failure, he is coming back a soldier who gambled his life and lost his health doing it. The phrase “to complete what was lacking in your service to me” is not a rebuke of Philippian stinginess; what was lacking was simply the one thing some eight hundred miles prevented them from sending, their own presence.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be cheered by news of you. For I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be cheered by news of you. For I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare.

I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon. Key words. Paul’s plans are in the Lord.

So that I too may be cheered by news of you. Key words. Timothy would bring back news.

For I have no one like him. Key words. “Like him” (isopsychos, of equal soul, like-minded). Timothy shares Paul’s heart.

Who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare. Key words. “Genuinely” (gnēsiōs, sincerely). Timothy embodies the humble mind of verse 4: looking to others’ interests.

What it does not mean. It does not mean no one else cared. It means Timothy was unique in his like-mindedness with Paul.

In a sentence. Paul hopes in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that he also may be cheered when he receives news about you. He has no one else like Timothy, who will show genuine concern for your welfare.

On a Tuesday. Be someone who genuinely cares for others’ welfare, like Timothy.

verseByVerse.quote: For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know Timothy’s proven worth, how as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel. I hope therefore to send him just as soon as I see how it will go with me, and I trust in the Lord that shortly I myself will come also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know Timothy’s proven worth, how as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel. I hope therefore to send him just as soon as I see how it will go with me, and I trust in the Lord that shortly I myself will come also.

For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. Key words. A sad comment on others around Paul. Self-interest is the opposite of the mind of Christ.

But you know Timothy’s proven worth. Key words. “Proven worth” (dokimē, tested character). The Philippians knew him from Paul’s first visit (Acts 16:1–3; 17:14).

How as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel. Key words. “Served” (douleuō, slaved). Like an apprentice son learning his father’s trade.

I hope therefore to send him just as soon as I see how it will go with me. Key words. After Paul’s trial outcome is known.

And I trust in the Lord that shortly I myself will come also. Key words. Paul expects release.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian around Paul was selfish. Some were faithful, like Epaphroditus.

In a sentence. For everyone looks out for their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know that Timothy has proved himself, because as a son with his father he has served with Paul in the work of the gospel. Paul hopes, therefore, to send him as soon as he sees how things go with him. And he is confident in the Lord that he himself will come soon.

For worship. Thank God for spiritual fathers and sons, mentors and apprentices in the faith.

verseByVerse.quote: I have thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus my brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need, for he has been longing for you all and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. Indeed he was ill, near to death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus my brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier, and your messenger and minister to my need, for he has been longing for you all and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. Indeed he was ill, near to death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.

I have thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus. Key words. Epaphroditus had brought the Philippians’ gift to Paul (4:18). Now Paul sends him home, probably carrying this letter.

My brother and fellow worker and fellow soldier. Key words. Three titles of honour: family, partnership, shared battle.

And your messenger and minister to my need. Key words. “Messenger” (apostolos, sent one). “Minister” (leitourgos, priestly servant): his service was worship.

For he has been longing for you all and has been distressed because you heard that he was ill. Key words. “Distressed” (adēmoneō, deeply troubled), the word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). He was upset that they were worried about him.

Indeed he was ill, near to death. Key words. Seriously ill.

But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow. Key words. His recovery was God’s mercy. Paul does not say he healed him miraculously, though he had the gift. Paul admits he would have grieved deeply. Grief is not unbelief.

What it does not mean. It does not mean healing is automatic for those with faith. Paul could not heal at will; God showed mercy as he chose.

In a sentence. But Paul thinks it is necessary to send back to you Epaphroditus, his brother, co-worker and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger, whom you sent to take care of his needs. For he longs for all of you and is distressed because you heard he was ill. Indeed he was ill, and almost died. But God had mercy on him, and not on him only but also on Paul, to spare him sorrow upon sorrow.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for healing when it comes, and do not be ashamed to grieve.
verseByVerse.note: Epaphroditus had brought the Philippians’ gift to Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the more eager to send him, therefore, that you may rejoice at seeing him again, and that I may be less anxious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the more eager to send him, therefore, that you may rejoice at seeing him again, and that I may be less anxious.

I am the more eager to send him, therefore, that you may rejoice at seeing him again. Key words. Paul gives up the help of a dear friend so that the Philippians can rejoice. Looking to others’ interests.

And that I may be less anxious. Key words. Literally, less sorrowful. Paul will be relieved knowing they are reassured. Honest about his feelings.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul disobeyed his own command to be anxious for nothing (4:6). He felt concern and brought it to God.

In a sentence. Therefore Paul is all the more eager to send him, so that when you see him again you may be glad and he may have less anxiety.

For worship. Thank God for reunions with those you love.

verseByVerse.quote: So receive him in the Lord with all joy, and honor such men, for he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to complete what was lacking in your service to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So receive him in the Lord with all joy, and honor such men, for he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to complete what was lacking in your service to me.

So receive him in the Lord with all joy. Key words. Not with disappointment that he came home early, but with joy.

And honor such men. Key words. People who risk themselves for Christ deserve honour.

For he nearly died for the work of Christ. Key words. His illness came through his service.

Risking his life. Key words. “Risking” (paraboleuomai, gambling, staking). In the early church, a group called the parabolani, the gamblers, risked their lives caring for plague victims, named from this word.

To complete what was lacking in your service to me. Key words. The Philippians could not be there in person; Epaphroditus served on their behalf.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Philippians had failed. They could not be present; he represented them.

In a sentence. So then, welcome him in the Lord with great joy, and honour people like him, because he almost died for the work of Christ. He risked his life to make up for the help you yourselves could not give Paul.

On a Tuesday. Honour those who risk much for Christ. Pray for those serving in danger.
